stage_description: The adult stage spans from about five weeks to one year, when the mouse is fully grown and in its prime. Sexual maturity is complete, body size is at its peak, and behaviour settles into a stable pattern: females remain sociable while males become more territorial. On the mouse-to-human scale, this year corresponds to the prime adult years of a person.
nutrition: Feed a complete formulated mouse diet, preferring uniform blocks or pellets over fatty, seed-heavy mixes that encourage obesity and selective feeding. Add only small amounts of fresh vegetables and occasional treats, and keep fresh water available at all times. Scatter or hide food to encourage natural foraging, and monitor weight.
activity: Keep the environment rich with a wheel, tunnels, ropes, climbing structures, a digging area, and foraging and chew toys, all in secure, well-ventilated housing away from drafts. Handle your mouse regularly to maintain the bond. Females do best in same-sex groups, while males usually must live alone to avoid serious fighting.
veterinary_check_frequency: Schedule a wellness exam with an exotics or rodent-savvy veterinarian at least once a year; given the short lifespan, every six months is even better. Weigh your mouse regularly at home and run a gentle lump check, and discuss diet and housing at each visit.
dental_care: The continuously growing incisors need constant gnawing material such as wood chews, mineral blocks, and cardboard. Check the incisors regularly for overgrowth or misalignment; signs of trouble include weight loss, drooling, and dropping food. A vet can trim overgrown teeth.
warning_signs: See an exotics vet for sneezing, wheezing, clicking, or laboured breathing, red staining around the eyes or nose, and any lump or swelling, since mammary tumours are common in females. Weight or appetite loss, diarrhoea, a head tilt, and lethargy also warrant an examination.
disclaimer: This information is for educational purposes only and does not replace consultation with a veterinarian.
